name: Form, place and finish concrete
summary: A self-perform concrete crew builds the forms and shoring for one pour, waits for the rebar subcontractor and the trades to place reinforcing and embeds, passes the foreman's check, the formwork engineer's pre-pour inspection and the engineer of record's rebar review, then places, finishes and cures the concrete and strips the forms once it is strong enough. Foremen, carpenters, labourers, finishers and the tower crane operator do the work; outside engineers, testing technicians and ready-mix suppliers control the pace. Weather, late trucks, failed inspections and waiting for strength before stripping stretch the cycle and tie up formwork sets.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor of about 2,800 people with union concrete and formwork crews that self-perform structural concrete on its own building projects.
baseline.notes: One pour is one placement: a footing run, a set of walls or columns, a slab on grade or a suspended deck. Touch time on crew steps is the crew's elapsed working time, not person-minutes.

trigger: The weekly crew plan assigns a concrete crew to a pour on a project.
end_state: The concrete is placed, finished and cured, forms are stripped (and re-shored where needed) and cycled or returned, and the pour record is closed. Twenty-eight-day strength results arrive later and are handled by quality inspection.

volume.seasonality: Pours peak from May to October; winter pours need hoarding and heat and drop by about a third.

evidence.note: Org file process map estimate: about 75 concrete crews doing about two pours a week each.

surge.cause: construction season (May to October), when concrete, earthworks and exterior work peak

evidence.note: Seasonal pattern of Canadian concrete work, as in the org file.
About 90 foremen in the org file; most of their time is on forming and pouring, the rest on general works. FTE is the author's estimate.
40 general foremen in the org file split between concrete placement, crew planning and general works; estimate.
480 carpenters in the org file; about 400 FTE on forming and stripping for pours, the rest on general works and carpentry; estimate.
380 labourers in the org file; about 170 FTE attached to concrete crews; estimate.
120 finishers in the org file; estimate.
Tower crane operators spend most of their hours on pour-cycle lifts (forms, rebar bundles, buckets); estimate.

systems.name: Project management platform (drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events)
Equipment management (fleet register, rates, maintenance work orders)
Safety management system (hazard assessments, inspections, incidents, training records)
Field time capture (paper sheets or tablet app keyed to cost codes)

resources.name: Concrete and formwork crews (foreman plus 6 to 12 trades)
Formwork systems (table forms, gang forms, shoring sets)
Telehandlers, skid steers and aerial work platforms

steps.name: Review pour package and sequence
steps.description: The foreman opens the crew assignment, the structural drawings, the reviewed rebar and formwork shop drawings and the pour sequence on the project platform, and works out the forms, shoring, crew size and pour volume for this placement. He notes embedded items, construction joints and any missing information to raise with the superintendent.

error.defect_description: Embedded item or joint missed on the work plan.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Confirm engineered formwork drawings on site
steps.description: The general foreman checks that the formwork, falsework and re-shoring design drawings stamped by the formwork engineer cover this pour, match the current structural revision and are on site. If they are missing or out of date he asks the formwork engineer for a revision and holds the work.

control.basis: O. Reg. 213/91 ss. 89(2), 90 and 92: formwork, falsework and re-shoring designed by an engineer, design drawings kept on the project while in use

next.condition: revision requested from the formwork engineer

steps.name: Request formwork, equipment and crane time
steps.description: The foreman calls or emails the yard for the formwork sets and shoring, sends an equipment request for telehandlers and pumps or buckets, asks for tower crane time in the daily crane schedule and raises a material requisition for ties, form oil, chairs and curing supplies.

error.defect_description: Wrong quantity or wrong form type ordered.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Lay out gridlines and set out forms
steps.description: Two carpenters take the gridlines and elevations from the field engineer's survey control, snap lines and set bottom plates, sill plates or edge forms. Touch time is elapsed working time for the pair; the wait before is forms and telehandlers arriving from the yard.

error.defect_description: Layout off grid or wrong elevation.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Hold pre-task hazard assessment with crew
steps.description: The foreman walks the crew through the formwork task on the hazard assessment form: fall protection at the leading edge, crane loads overhead, material handling and access. Each worker signs the form, which goes to the site safety coordinator.

control.basis: Company health and safety program: daily field-level hazard assessment before work starts (COR program element)

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Erect forms, shoring and edge protection
steps.description: Carpenters build the wall, column or deck forms, set shores and stringers to the engineered layout, install edge protection and openings and oil the form faces. Touch time is elapsed working time for a crew of 4 to 10 carpenters; a small footing takes part of a day and a large suspended deck takes most of a week.

error.defect_description: Shore spacing, bracing, tie or alignment deviates from the drawings.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Move material and clean forms for carpenters
steps.description: Labourers unload and stage plywood, shores and ties, clean and oil form panels, carry material to the deck and keep the work area clear while the carpenters build. Touch time is elapsed working time for the one to three labourers attached to the crew.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Rebar subcontractor places reinforcing
steps.description: The rebar subcontractor's rodmen place and tie the reinforcing steel and dowels to the reviewed bar placing drawings once the forms are ready. The self-perform crew waits for them or moves to other work.

error.defect_description: Missing bars, wrong cover or wrong lap length.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Trades install sleeves and embedded services
steps.description: Mechanical and electrical subcontractors set sleeves, conduit, boxes and embedded plates in the forms while the rebar goes in. The foreman checks with their foremen that every embed on the coordination drawing is in.

error.defect_description: Sleeve or conduit missing or in the wrong place.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Foreman pre-pour check
steps.description: The foreman walks the forms with a tape and level and checks dimensions, elevations, shoring, ties, embeds, cleanliness and access for the pump or bucket, and fills in the company pre-pour checklist. He sends the inspection request for the formwork and rebar inspections.

control.basis: Company quality plan: foreman pre-pour checklist before requesting inspection

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Formwork engineer inspects before the pour
steps.description: The formwork engineer, or a competent worker the engineer has designated in writing, inspects the formwork and falsework against the design drawings and signs a written statement that it is built as designed. This applies to shored decks and tall forms; for simple footings the superintendent's own check stands in.

control.basis: O. Reg. 213/91 s. 89(3)-(4): engineer or designated competent worker inspects formwork and falsework before concrete is placed and states in writing that it matches the design drawings

evidence.note: Share of pours needing rework is an estimate.

steps.name: Engineer of record reviews the reinforcing
steps.description: The structural engineer of record's field reviewer, or the inspection and testing company, checks bar sizes, spacing, cover and laps against the drawings and issues a field review report. Defects go back to the rebar subcontractor and the crew.

control.basis: Contract specification and Ontario Building Code general review: structural engineer of record reviews reinforcing before concrete is placed

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Correct form, shoring or rebar deficiencies
steps.description: Carpenters add missing shores or braces, re-align forms, fix ties or clean out debris, and the rebar subcontractor corrects bars where needed. The foreman then asks for the inspection again.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Order concrete and pump
steps.description: The foreman phones the ready-mix dispatcher against the supplier purchase order, confirms the mix design, volume, slump, start time and truck spacing, and books the concrete pump or confirms crane time for bucket placement. He also books the testing company technician.

error.defect_description: Wrong mix, volume or start time ordered.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Check forecast and confirm the pour
steps.description: The general foreman reviews the forecast the evening before and early on pour day for rain, wind for crane work and cold below 5 C, checks heaters, blankets and hoarding are ready, and confirms or cancels the trucks and pump. A cancelled pour waits for the next suitable day.

next.condition: postponed for rain, wind or cold

evidence.note: Postponement share is an estimate for a Canadian building contractor across the year; higher in spring and late fall.

steps.name: Pre-pour meeting and set up placing equipment
steps.description: The foreman briefs the placing crew, pump operator, crane operator and finishers on the pour sequence, washout, signals, exclusion zones under the boom and bucket, and who stops the pour if forms move. The crew sets out vibrators, screeds and walkways.

control.basis: Pre-job safety meeting and O. Reg. 213/91 ss. 104 and 106: signaller for crane and pump boom when the operator's view is blocked

steps.name: Place and consolidate concrete
steps.description: Labourers guide the pump hose or bucket, spread and vibrate the concrete in lifts and watch for honeycombing, while a carpenter watches the forms for movement. Trucks that arrive late leave the crew standing; touch time is elapsed placing time for a crew of 4 to 6.

error.defect_description: Cold joint, honeycombing or poor consolidation.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Operate tower crane for bucket placement
steps.description: Where the pump cannot reach, the tower crane operator flies the concrete bucket from the truck to the deck on the signaller's direction. Most pours are pumped and this step takes little or no crane time.

evidence.note: Share of pours placed by bucket (about a third) is an estimate.

steps.name: Testing company samples the concrete
steps.description: The testing technician checks slump, air content and temperature on the first truck and at the specified frequency, and casts cylinders for 7-day and 28-day strength. A truck that fails slump or air is rejected and sent back.

control.basis: CSA A23.1/A23.2 field testing by a certified technician; air content tested with every set of cylinders

evidence.note: Testing practice summarised from the CFCA article; frequency is from the project specification.

steps.name: Finish and protect the surface
steps.description: Finishers screed, bull-float and power-trowel slabs to the specified flatness once bleed water has gone, and patch and rub wall ties where required. Walls and footings need little finishing; touch time is elapsed time for a finishing crew of 3 to 5.

error.defect_description: Surface out of flatness tolerance or burned.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Cure and protect from cold or heat
steps.description: Labourers place curing compound, wet burlap or poly, and in cold weather set insulated blankets, hoarding and heaters and log concrete temperatures so the concrete stays at 10 C or more for the curing period.

error.defect_description: Concrete allowed to freeze or dry out.

control.basis: CSA A23.1 cold-weather protection and curing: concrete kept at 10 C or more for three or seven days, as written into the project specification

steps.name: Record the pour in the daily report and timesheets
steps.description: The foreman writes the pour into the daily report (location, volume, trucks, weather, problems) and codes the crew's hours to the concrete cost codes in the timekeeping app or on paper sheets.

error.defect_description: Hours coded to the wrong cost code.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Confirm strength before stripping
steps.description: The general foreman waits for the curing period and the early cylinder or field-cured results from the testing company and decides with the engineer when forms and shores can come out. Walls strip in a day or two, suspended decks after several days and only with re-shores.

control.basis: O. Reg. 213/91 s. 88: forms and falsework not removed until the concrete can support itself and applied loads or is adequately re-shored

evidence.note: Waiting time is the author's estimate; the regulation sets no fixed period.

steps.name: Strip forms and install re-shores
steps.description: Carpenters strip wall and column forms or fly the deck tables, install re-shores to the engineer's re-shoring layout under suspended slabs and send the panels to the next pour. Touch time is elapsed time for a crew of 3 to 6.

control.basis: O. Reg. 213/91 s. 90: re-shoring designed by an engineer and installed to the design drawings

steps.name: Clean, sort and cycle or return forms
steps.description: Labourers scrape and oil panels, sort ties and hardware, stack forms for the next pour or load damaged and surplus sets for return to the yard.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Close the pour record
steps.description: The foreman files the inspection statements, test reports, delivery tickets and pour card in the project platform and reports the poured quantity so the cost report shows units in place.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Engineer investigates low strength
steps.description: The engineer of record asks for field-cured results, cores or rebound tests and reviews them against design strength. The pour stays shored until the engineer accepts it or orders a repair.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Carry out remedial work
steps.description: Carpenters and labourers remove and replace a small section, add supplementary support or prepare the surface for an engineered repair, as the engineer's disposition directs, and then strip the remaining forms.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

exceptions.name: Failed pre-pour inspection
exceptions.description: The foreman, the formwork engineer or the rebar reviewer finds missing shores, braces, bars or embeds; the crew fixes them and the inspection is repeated, often pushing the pour a day.

exceptions.name: Pour postponed for weather
exceptions.description: Rain, high wind or a cold forecast cancels the trucks and pump; the formed and inspected pour waits for the next workable day while the formwork set stays tied up.

exceptions.name: Low early strength
exceptions.description: Early cylinders come in low; the deck stays shored while the engineer reviews cores and decides whether a repair is needed.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from crew assignment to forms stripped and pour record closed
benchmarks.population: Mix of footing, wall, column, slab-on-grade and suspended deck pours on Canadian building projects, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: walls and footings turn in 3 to 6 days, a suspended deck on a 5 to 7 day floor cycle plus several days before stripping. No published benchmark was found.
Sized so that 600 pours a month use about three quarters of the concrete division's available hours.

pain_points.description: Formwork and rebar inspections are booked with outside engineers and often fail on small items, so the crew re-works and the pour slips a day.

evidence.note: Common site complaint; estimate.

pain_points.description: Pours wait on weather and on ready-mix truck spacing; crews stand idle when trucks are late.

evidence.note: Estimate.

pain_points.description: Formwork sets sit under curing concrete for days, so the number of sets limits how fast a crew can cycle floors.

evidence.note: Stripping depends on strength or re-shoring under s. 88; holding time is an estimate.

pain_points.description: Hours are coded to cost codes on paper or in an app at day end and are often wrong, which distorts unit-cost reports.

evidence.note: Estimate.

sources.supports: O. Reg. 213/91 ss. 87-92: formwork, falsework and re-shoring designed by an engineer (s. 89(2), s. 90); design drawings kept on the project (ss. 89(5), 92(2)); inspection before concrete is placed by an engineer or a competent worker designated in writing by the engineer, with a written statement (s. 89(3)-(4)); forms not removed until the concrete supports itself or is re-shored, with no fixed waiting period (s. 88); footings protected from frost heave (s. 91).

sources.title: Rigging | IHSA Construction Safety App
sources.supports: O. Reg. 213/91 crane and hoisting rules: operator certificates by crane type and capacity (s. 150(1)); signaller when the operator's view is blocked, competent and doing no other work (ss. 104, 106); weekly cable inspection recorded in the crane log (s. 170); engineer inspection of tower crane climbing systems before first climb and every 12 months (s. 159); competent-worker inspection of tower crane shoring and bracing before and after each climb and weekly (s. 157(13)); minimum distances and written procedures near energized overhead lines (s. 188).

sources.title: Concrete Floor Contractors Association Study - 2014 Concrete Materials Lab Test Study
sources.publisher: Concrete Floor Contractors Association (via Naylor Network)
sources.supports: CSA A23.1-2019 requires concrete materials to be kept at 10 C or more for the curing period of three or seven days; air content tested with every set of cylinders. Article date not stated; it cites the 2019 edition.

assumptions: Crew-step touch times are the crew's elapsed working minutes at the step, so the simulated cycle time is not inflated by adding up every crew member's minutes. Person-hours are touch time times crew size (stated in each step description): about 190 person-hours for a typical pour against about 80 hours of elapsed crew time. Simulated labour cost per pour therefore counts one person per step and understates crew cost by a factor of about 3 to 5; resource occupied_min for concrete-crew and finishing-crew gives the crew hours.

Reinforcing steel is placed by a rebar subcontractor, as is common for Ontario building contractors; the self-perform crew forms, places, finishes and strips. The org file's self-perform page (Bird) lists concrete but not rebar.
Outside parties (rebar subcontractor, formwork engineer, engineer of record, testing company) are modelled as external waits with no touch time, so their effort is not in the staffing check.

Stated FTE (790) is above the validator's implied FTE because touch time counts one crew's elapsed time, not every member's hours; 600 pours at about 190 person-hours use about 114,000 person-hours a month, about 870 FTE at 130 productive hours or about 650 at the 175 hours trades work in season.

Simulated median cycle time (about 15 days) is about 1.5 times the tier C benchmark of 10 days. The simulator adds concurrent steps in sequence (labourers alongside carpenters, crane and testing alongside placing, embeds alongside rebar), and one set of triangular ranges mixes very different pour types, which also makes the simulated p90 (about 18 days) narrower than real spread; footings and walls sit at the low end and suspended decks at the high end.
The organisation's process map does not list the testing agency as an input or the rebar subcontractor; the workflow adds test_report from testing-agency as an input.
O. Reg. 213/91 sections are cited from the IHSA summary of the current text; these formwork and crane sections were in force in substantially the same form in 2019-2022.
